sources.document_name: AI fictional teaching passage: a curator's account
sources.text: This passage and all its people, places and events are fictional, written by an AI assistant for a teaching exercise. The curator of the imagined North Quay community archive writes: We finally opened the exhibition together. Volunteers carried boxes from their homes, and children stopped before the wall of photographs. We chose captions short enough to read in a crowded room. The opening felt like a beginning, not a finished history. The passage is narrated by someone responsible for the exhibition. It does not identify who selected the photographs, list rejected contributions, or report every visitor's reaction.

sources.document_name: AI fictional teaching passage: a volunteer's account
sources.text: This is an AI-authored fictional companion passage, not a real interview or archival quotation. A volunteer from the same imagined exhibition writes: I recognized my father's coat in a photograph, though the caption named only the factory. I was glad that someone had kept the picture. When the curator thanked us, I applauded, but I kept the letter I had brought inside my bag. Perhaps there would be another occasion to show it. The narrator reports gratitude and hesitation but does not state why the letter was withheld, whether anybody rejected it, or what it contained.

sources.document_name: AI-authored teaching note: perspective and interpretive limits
sources.text: A first-person account gives access to a situated viewpoint, not automatic knowledge of every participant's motives. Distinguish a narrator's explicit statement from an inference based on an image, omission or contrast. The curator's collective we can be read as an aspiration to shared ownership or as a phrase that leaves differences within the group unstated. The volunteer's applause and unopened letter can support readings of tentative belonging, unresolved exclusion, or a mixture, but the text does not establish censorship or identify the letter's contents. A defensible interpretation compares details from both passages, acknowledges a plausible competing reading, and explains the limits of its claim. Different interpretations can meet these standards without using identical wording or agreeing on a single hidden intention.

Passage A - curator's account (Source ID: fiction_archive_curator_en):
This passage and all its people, places and events are fictional, written by an AI assistant for a teaching exercise. The curator of the imagined North Quay community archive writes:
We finally opened the exhibition together. Volunteers carried boxes from their homes, and children stopped before the wall of photographs. We chose captions short enough to read in a crowded room. The opening felt like a beginning, not a finished history.
The passage is narrated by someone responsible for the exhibition. It does not identify who selected the photographs, list rejected contributions, or report every visitor's reaction.

Passage B - volunteer's account (Source ID: fiction_archive_volunteer_en):
This is an AI-authored fictional companion passage, not a real interview or archival quotation. A volunteer from the same imagined exhibition writes:
I recognized my father's coat in a photograph, though the caption named only the factory. I was glad that someone had kept the picture. When the curator thanked us, I applauded, but I kept the letter I had brought inside my bag. Perhaps there would be another occasion to show it.
The narrator reports gratitude and hesitation but does not state why the letter was withheld, whether anybody rejected it, or what it contained.

Passage C - teaching note (Source ID: fiction_archive_method_en):
A first-person account gives access to a situated viewpoint, not automatic knowledge of every participant's motives. Distinguish a narrator's explicit statement from an inference based on an image, omission or contrast. The curator's collective we can be read as an aspiration to shared ownership or as a phrase that leaves differences within the group unstated. The volunteer's applause and unopened letter can support readings of tentative belonging, unresolved exclusion, or a mixture, but the text does not establish censorship or identify the letter's contents. A defensible interpretation compares details from both passages, acknowledges a plausible competing reading, and explains the limits of its claim. Different interpretations can meet these standards without using identical wording or agreeing on a single hidden intention.

1. State whether a first-person account gives direct access to every participant's motives or only a situated viewpoint, and use Passage C to support your point.
2. Cite at least one specific detail from Passage A and explain what it does and does not establish.
3. Contrast the volunteer's applause with the kept, unshown letter in Passage B, and explain how that pairing can support more than one reading of belonging.
4. Defend an interpretation of the exhibition's shared-ownership claim, and engage one plausible competing reading of the same details.
5. Keep all claims within Passages A-C: do not assert censorship, hidden motives, or the letter's contents; flag uncertainty where the passages are silent.
6. Explain the limits of your reading and what further evidence would be needed to settle the question of differing perspectives.

Question: Based on the supplied passages, write a defensible interpretation of how the curator's and the volunteer's first-person accounts differ in perspective. Address each numbered condition in your response.","options":[],"answer":"A defensible response could argue that the two accounts differ mainly in what each narrator can see and say from their position, not in reporting contradictory events.

Passage C establishes the limit: first-person narration gives a situated viewpoint, not automatic access to every participant's motives. The curator can report the opening, the volunteers carrying boxes, the children stopping before the photographs, and the choice of short captions, but cannot establish that everyone experienced shared ownership.

The curator's collective 'we' can be read as an aspiration to shared ownership: 'We finally opened the exhibition together' and 'We chose captions short enough to read in a crowded room' present the exhibition as jointly made. The same details do not identify who selected the photographs, list rejected contributions, or report every visitor's reaction. So the 'we' supports attempted inclusion more reliably than it proves equal authority or unanimous agreement.

The volunteer's account complicates that picture. The volunteer applauds when the curator thanks the group, which supports a reading of gratitude and tentative belonging. Yet the volunteer also keeps the letter inside the bag: 'I kept the letter I had brought inside my bag.' That pairing can support more than one reading: (a) the volunteer feels enough belonging to applaud but remains only partly included; or (b) the applause is social participation that coexists with a private, unresolved relationship to the exhibition. Passage C permits both and adds a third possibility, a mixture, without establishing censorship.

A plausible competing reading is that the accounts do not really conflict. Both show an opening that is collaborative and unfinished, and the volunteer's withheld letter may simply be saved for 'another occasion to show it' rather than evidence of exclusion. The volunteer was glad someone kept the picture, and the passage does not state why the letter was withheld or whether anyone rejected it.

The limits of any interpretation are therefore significant. The passages do not report every visitor's reaction, identify rejected contributions, explain the letter's contents, or say whether the letter was withheld because of exclusion, privacy, timing, or another reason. To settle the question of differing perspectives, further evidence would be needed: records of who selected the photographs, an account of rejected or unshown contributions, the volunteer's own explanation for keeping the letter, and other participants' reactions. function.description:
Deterministic single-processor RR or STCF scheduling with independent, single-burst processes and no I/O. Times are integer abstract time units. Initial dispatch and dispatch after an idle interval are free. RR boundary=before/after orders arrivals exactly at a slice end before/after the unfinished process is requeued; earlier waiting processes keep their position. during_switch=tail appends switch-time arrivals to the queue; before_preempted inserts them immediately before the just-preempted process if it is still queued, otherwise at the tail. The next process is selected before switching, and arrivals through the switch end are enqueued before it starts. early_finish_free waives the next different-process switch cost only if the previous process completed in less than a full quantum. Same-process continuation is free. STCF supports zero switch cost only and chooses (remaining time, id), including id-based preemption on equal remaining times. Id comparison is Unicode lexicographic order. switch_count counts adjacent different-process transitions, including free early-finish transitions, but excludes initial/idle dispatch. makespan is final completion measured from time zero, including initial and intermediate idle intervals. Consecutive run intervals for the same process without an intervening switch/idle interval are merged.

function.name: mcp__teaching__cpu_schedule_v1
function.description:
Deterministic single-processor RR or STCF scheduling with independent, single-burst processes and no I/O. Times are integer abstract time units. Initial dispatch and dispatch after an idle interval are free. RR boundary=before/after orders arrivals exactly at a slice end before/after the unfinished process is requeued; earlier waiting processes keep their position. during_switch=tail appends switch-time arrivals to the queue; before_preempted inserts them immediately before the just-preempted process if it is still queued, otherwise at the tail. The next process is selected before switching, and arrivals through the switch end are enqueued before it starts. early_finish_free waives the next different-process switch cost only if the previous process completed in less than a full quantum. Same-process continuation is free. STCF supports zero switch cost only and chooses (remaining time, id), including id-based preemption on equal remaining times. Id comparison is Unicode lexicographic order. switch_count counts adjacent different-process transitions, including free early-finish transitions, but excludes initial/idle dispatch. makespan is final completion measured from time zero, including initial and intermediate idle intervals. Consecutive run intervals for the same process without an intervening switch/idle interval are merged.

questions.stem:
Background: The North Quay community archive exhibition is entirely fictional; this exercise uses only the three AI-authored passages supplied below.

Passage A - curator's account (Source ID: fiction_archive_curator_en):
This passage and all its people, places and events are fictional, written by an AI assistant for a teaching exercise. The curator of the imagined North Quay community archive writes:
We finally opened the exhibition together. Volunteers carried boxes from their homes, and children stopped before the wall of photographs. We chose captions short enough to read in a crowded room. The opening felt like a beginning, not a finished history.
The passage is narrated by someone responsible for the exhibition. It does not identify who selected the photographs, list rejected contributions, or report every visitor's reaction.

Passage B - volunteer's account (Source ID: fiction_archive_volunteer_en):
This is an AI-authored fictional companion passage, not a real interview or archival quotation. A volunteer from the same imagined exhibition writes:
I recognized my father's coat in a photograph, though the caption named only the factory. I was glad that someone had kept the picture. When the curator thanked us, I applauded, but I kept the letter I had brought inside my bag. Perhaps there would be another occasion to show it.
The narrator reports gratitude and hesitation but does not state why the letter was withheld, whether anybody rejected it, or what it contained.

Passage C - teaching note (Source ID: fiction_archive_method_en):
A first-person account gives access to a situated viewpoint, not automatic knowledge of every participant's motives. Distinguish a narrator's explicit statement from an inference based on an image, omission or contrast. The curator's collective we can be read as an aspiration to shared ownership or as a phrase that leaves differences within the group unstated. The volunteer's applause and unopened letter can support readings of tentative belonging, unresolved exclusion, or a mixture, but the text does not establish censorship or identify the letter's contents. A defensible interpretation compares details from both passages, acknowledges a plausible competing reading, and explains the limits of its claim. Different interpretations can meet these standards without using identical wording or agreeing on a single hidden intention.

1. State whether a first-person account gives direct access to every participant's motives or only a situated viewpoint, and use Passage C to support your point.
2. Cite at least one specific detail from Passage A and explain what it does and does not establish.
3. Contrast the volunteer's applause with the kept, unshown letter in Passage B, and explain how that pairing can support more than one reading of belonging.
4. Defend an interpretation of the exhibition's shared-ownership claim, and engage one plausible competing reading of the same details.
5. Keep all claims within Passages A-C: do not assert censorship, hidden motives, or the letter's contents; flag uncertainty where the passages are silent.
6. Explain the limits of your reading and what further evidence would be needed to settle the question of differing perspectives.

Question: Based on the supplied passages, write a defensible interpretation of how the curator's and the volunteer's first-person accounts differ in perspective. Address each numbered condition in your response.
questions.answer:
A defensible response could argue that the two accounts differ mainly in what each narrator can see and say from their position, not in reporting contradictory events.

Passage C establishes the limit: first-person narration gives a situated viewpoint, not automatic access to every participant's motives. The curator can report the opening, the volunteers carrying boxes, the children stopping before the photographs, and the choice of short captions, but cannot establish that everyone experienced shared ownership.

The curator's collective 'we' can be read as an aspiration to shared ownership: 'We finally opened the exhibition together' and 'We chose captions short enough to read in a crowded room' present the exhibition as jointly made. The same details do not identify who selected the photographs, list rejected contributions, or report every visitor's reaction. So the 'we' supports attempted inclusion more reliably than it proves equal authority or unanimous agreement.

The volunteer's account complicates that picture. The volunteer applauds when the curator thanks the group, which supports a reading of gratitude and tentative belonging. Yet the volunteer also keeps the letter inside the bag: 'I kept the letter I had brought inside my bag.' That pairing can support more than one reading: (a) the volunteer feels enough belonging to applaud but remains only partly included; or (b) the applause is social participation that coexists with a private, unresolved relationship to the exhibition. Passage C permits both and adds a third possibility, a mixture, without establishing censorship.

A plausible competing reading is that the accounts do not really conflict. Both show an opening that is collaborative and unfinished, and the volunteer's withheld letter may simply be saved for 'another occasion to show it' rather than evidence of exclusion. The volunteer was glad someone kept the picture, and the passage does not state why the letter was withheld or whether anyone rejected it.

The limits of any interpretation are therefore significant. The passages do not report every visitor's reaction, identify rejected contributions, explain the letter's contents, or say whether the letter was withheld because of exclusion, privacy, timing, or another reason. To settle the question of differing perspectives, further evidence would be needed: records of who selected the photographs, an account of rejected or unshown contributions, the volunteer's own explanation for keeping the letter, and other participants' reactions. Even with that evidence, the reading would remain an interpretation of situated accounts.
questions.explanation: Full-credit answers should do the following: state that first-person narration is situated and does not give access to every motive (fiction_archive_method_en); cite a specific curator detail such as the collective 'we' or the short captions and separate what it reports from what it proves (fiction_archive_curator_en); contrast the volunteer's applause with the kept, unshown letter and explain how that pairing supports tentative belonging, unresolved exclusion, or a mixture (fiction_archive_volunteer_en; fiction_archive_method_en); defend a reading of shared ownership while engaging a plausible competing reading; and explicitly avoid claiming censorship, hidden motives, or the letter's contents, naming what further evidence would be needed. Different wordings and different final weightings are acceptable if they meet these conditions.

No outside historical or theoretical sources are needed.","learning_objectives":[],"section_scope":"shared","sections":[],"questions":[{"slot_id":"q1","difficulty":"hard","difficulty_design":{"cognitive_process":"evaluate","concepts":["First-person perspective","Explicit statement versus inference","Textual omission and uncertainty","Competing interpretations","Evidentiary limits"],"expected_steps":["Identify each narrator's situated first-person position and separate explicit statements from inferences.","Use a specific detail from the curator's account, such as the collective we or the short captions, and state what it does and does not establish.","Contrast the volunteer's applause with the kept, unshown letter and explain how the pairing supports more than one reading of belonging or exclusion.","Defend a bounded judgment on shared ownership while engaging a plausible counterargument.","State the limits of the reading and what further evidence would be needed, without asserting censorship, motive or the letter's contents."]},"kind":"short_answer","stem":"Background: This is a fictional teaching exercise. The people, places and events are invented. The excerpts below are the entire evidence you may use.

Passage 1 — curator's account:
'We finally opened the exhibition together. Volunteers carried boxes from their homes, and children stopped before the wall of photographs. We chose captions short enough to read in a crowded room. The opening felt like a beginning, not a finished history.'

Passage 2 — volunteer's account:
'I recognized my father's coat in a photograph, though the caption named only the factory. I was glad that someone had kept the picture. When the curator thanked us, I applauded, but I kept the letter I had brought inside my bag. Perhaps there would be another occasion to show it.'

Passage 3 — method note:
'A first-person account gives access to a situated viewpoint, not automatic knowledge of every participant's motives. Distinguish a narrator's explicit statement from an inference based on an image, omission or contrast. The curator's collective we can be read as an aspiration to shared ownership or as a phrase that leaves differences within the group unstated. The volunteer's applause and unopened letter can support readings of tentative belonging, unresolved exclusion, or a mixture, but the text does not establish censorship or identify the letter's contents. A defensible interpretation compares details from both passages, acknowledges a plausible competing reading, and explains the limits of its claim. Different interpretations can meet these standards without using identical wording or agreeing on a single hidden intention.'

Conditions:
1. Use only the three passages above; do not add outside history, theory or facts about real archives.
2. Do not assert what the passages leave open: the letter's contents, the volunteer's motive for keeping it, whether anyone rejected or censored the letter, or how other visitors felt.
3. Compare both first-person accounts. A response that discusses only the curator or only the volunteer is incomplete.
4. Include at least one plausible counterargument to your own judgment.
5. End by naming what further evidence would be needed to settle the disagreement about shared ownership.

Two classmates disagree. Alex argues that the exhibition achieved shared ownership: the curator's 'we' and the volunteer's applause show that the community made the exhibition together. Blair argues that the same details show unresolved exclusion: the volunteer kept the letter in his bag, so the exhibition failed to include what mattered.

Write a response that adjudicates between Alex and Blair. State and defend a bounded judgment about how much shared ownership the passages support, or explain why neither claim is fully defensible. Support your judgment with specific details from both accounts, and satisfy conditions 1-5.","options":[],"answer":"Source facts: Both passages are first-person accounts. The curator writes 'We finally opened the exhibition together,' says 'We chose captions short enough to read in a crowded room,' and calls the opening 'a beginning, not a finished history.' The volunteer writes that he applauded when the curator thanked the volunteers but 'kept the letter I had brought inside my bag,' hoping for 'another occasion to show it.' The method note states that first-person narration gives a situated viewpoint, not access to everyone's motives, and that the text does not establish censorship or the letter's contents.

Supported inferences: The curator's collective 'we' can be read as an aspiration to shared ownership, because it describes joint opening and caption choices. It does not prove that all community members felt included or that every contribution was displayed. The volunteer's applause can be read as public agreement or gratitude, while the kept letter can be read as hesitation, privacy, or a sense that the moment was not right. Neither detail shows that anyone rejected the letter.

Bounded judgment: A defensible verdict is mixed and partial. Alex's shared-ownership reading is stronger on the public, collective evidence: the curator's 'we' and the volunteer's applause show collaboration and at least momentary belonging. Blair's exclusion reading is stronger on the unshown letter, which marks something withheld from the exhibition. The passages support 'shared ownership underway but incomplete' better than either full shared ownership or outright exclusion. The strongest claim is that the exhibition created a public shared space while one participant kept part of his archive private.

Counterargument: A reader could reply that the kept letter is irrelevant to the exhibition's inclusiveness because the volunteer may simply have chosen not to show it, so Alex's reading stands. That is possible, but the contrast between public applause and private retention is still a textual detail that qualifies any claim of complete shared ownership; it does not prove exclusion, only incompleteness.

Limits and further evidence: The passages do not tell us why the letter was kept back, what it contained, whether anyone knew about it, whether other contributions were rejected, or how other visitors experienced the exhibition. To settle the disagreement, we would need evidence such as the volunteer's explicit explanation, records of what was offered or declined, or accounts from other participants. Until then, the judgment must remain bounded.","explanation":"A strong response treats both passages as situated first-person evidence. Alex's claim gains support from the curator's collective 'we' and the volunteer's applause, while Blair's claim gains support from the kept letter. The decisive move is to avoid asserting unstated motive, censorship or the letter's contents, and to explain why the evidence supports a mixed or bounded verdict rather than a complete one. The method note requires comparison, a competing reading and explicit limits, so a one-sided summary or a claim about the letter's contents would not satisfy the conditions.","difficulty_reason":"Students must integrate two first-person accounts with a method note, evaluate two competing claims under explicit constraints, and justify a bounded verdict without relying on unstated motives. The task requires weighing counterevidence and stating evidentiary limits, not recalling a definition.","citation_ids":["fiction_archive_curator_en","fiction_archive_volunteer_en","fiction_archive_method_en"]}],"visual_prompt":""}

questions.stem:
Background: This is a fictional teaching exercise. The people, places and events are invented. The excerpts below are the entire evidence you may use.

Passage 1 — curator's account:
'We finally opened the exhibition together. Volunteers carried boxes from their homes, and children stopped before the wall of photographs. We chose captions short enough to read in a crowded room. The opening felt like a beginning, not a finished history.'

Passage 2 — volunteer's account:
'I recognized my father's coat in a photograph, though the caption named only the factory. I was glad that someone had kept the picture. When the curator thanked us, I applauded, but I kept the letter I had brought inside my bag. Perhaps there would be another occasion to show it.'

Passage 3 — method note:
'A first-person account gives access to a situated viewpoint, not automatic knowledge of every participant's motives. Distinguish a narrator's explicit statement from an inference based on an image, omission or contrast. The curator's collective we can be read as an aspiration to shared ownership or as a phrase that leaves differences within the group unstated. The volunteer's applause and unopened letter can support readings of tentative belonging, unresolved exclusion, or a mixture, but the text does not establish censorship or identify the letter's contents. A defensible interpretation compares details from both passages, acknowledges a plausible competing reading, and explains the limits of its claim. Different interpretations can meet these standards without using identical wording or agreeing on a single hidden intention.'

Conditions:
1. Use only the three passages above; do not add outside history, theory or facts about real archives.
2. Do not assert what the passages leave open: the letter's contents, the volunteer's motive for keeping it, whether anyone rejected or censored the letter, or how other visitors felt.
3. Compare both first-person accounts. A response that discusses only the curator or only the volunteer is incomplete.
4. Include at least one plausible counterargument to your own judgment.
5. End by naming what further evidence would be needed to settle the disagreement about shared ownership.

Two classmates disagree. Alex argues that the exhibition achieved shared ownership: the curator's 'we' and the volunteer's applause show that the community made the exhibition together. Blair argues that the same details show unresolved exclusion: the volunteer kept the letter in his bag, so the exhibition failed to include what mattered.

Write a response that adjudicates between Alex and Blair. State and defend a bounded judgment about how much shared ownership the passages support, or explain why neither claim is fully defensible. Support your judgment with specific details from both accounts, and satisfy conditions 1-5.

brief.focus: Compare two accounts of a fictional archive exhibition and defend a bounded reading of perspective.
brief.learning_goal: Students will defend an interpretation of how the curator's and the volunteer's first-person accounts differ in perspective, using specific details, weighing a plausible competing reading, and limiting claims to what the passages actually establish.

requirements.description: State that a first-person account gives a situated viewpoint rather than access to every participant's motives or unstated intentions.
Cite a specific detail from the curator's account (such as the collective 'we' or the choice of short captions) and explain what it does and does not establish.
Contrast the volunteer's applause with the kept, unshown letter and explain how that pairing supports more than one reading of belonging.
Develop a defensible interpretation of the exhibition's shared-ownership claim and engage a plausible competing reading of the same details.
Keep claims within the passages: do not assert censorship, hidden motives or the letter's contents, and flag uncertainty where the text is silent.
Explain the limits of the chosen reading and what further evidence would be needed to settle the question of differing perspectives.

questions.focus: Compare two accounts of a fictional archive exhibition and defend a bounded reading of perspective.
questions.learning_goal: Students will defend an interpretation of how the curator's and the volunteer's first-person accounts differ in perspective, using specific details, weighing a plausible competing reading, and limiting claims to what the passages actually establish.

requirements.description: State that a first-person account gives a situated viewpoint rather than access to every participant's motives or unstated intentions.
Cite a specific detail from the curator's account (such as the collective 'we' or the choice of short captions) and explain what it does and does not establish.
Contrast the volunteer's applause with the kept, unshown letter and explain how that pairing supports more than one reading of belonging.
Develop a defensible interpretation of the exhibition's shared-ownership claim and engage a plausible competing reading of the same details.
Keep claims within the passages: do not assert censorship, hidden motives or the letter's contents, and flag uncertainty where the text is silent.
Explain the limits of the chosen reading and what further evidence would be needed to settle the question of differing perspectives.
